newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: PNG PM rejects reports of mercenary plan.
newsitem.headline: PNG PM rejects reports of mercenary plan.

text.p: Papua New Guinea Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan said on Monday media reports that his government planned to use mercenaries against secessionist rebels on Bougainville were inaccurate and sensationalism.
Chan said his South Pacific nation had hired Sandlines International, a private military training and logistical group, to help train government soldiers fighting on Bougainville.
"Yes there is training going on at the moment, training for our under-equipped, under-trained and under-resourced security forces," Chan said in a statement.
"I am sick and tired of our boys coming back in body bags."
Sandlines International is a subsidiary of the British-registered company Executive Outcomes -- Africa's best known private army and has helped Angola and Sierra Leone fight rebel threats.

"The team we have hired to train our security force members are not cowboys, they are a reputable professional company, who are part of our many faceted strategy to reach a lasting solution to this particular crisis...," Chan said.

Australian newspapers have reported Papua New Guinea planned to bring in up to 150 Africa-based mercenaries for an operation to capture or kill the leaders of the pro-independence Bougainville Revolutionary Army.
They said the government had approved a A$36-million (US$27-million) covert operation to end the nine-year rebellion on Bougainville, 800 km (500 miles) northeast of Port Moresby.

The media said military cargo aircraft leased to Sandlines International had been flying in and out of Jackson Airport in Port Moresby last week and that the mercenaries planned a "surgical strike" against Bougainville rebels.
Papua New Guinea Defence Force Chief-of-Staff Colonel Jack Tuat earlier said the latest training was no different to that involving Australia, New Zealand and the United States.

"We are occasionally bringing in people to train our guys on the use of new and specific equipment," Tuat told Reuters. "The training is part of capacity building by the defence forces to be able to contain any security problem."
The reports prompted Australia to warn Papua New Guinea against using mercenaries in Bougainville.
"We would regard the use of mercenaries as an extremely unwelcome development in the South Pacific," Australian Prime Minister John Howard told the Australian parliament on Monday.
Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer said he had warned Chan last week not to use mercenaries, adding such a move would significantly damage the country's international standing.
"I will use any vehicle which is reasonable that I possibly can to try to stop this operation going ahead..., he said.
Chan criticised Howard and Downer for reacting to the media reports, saying the plan to use non-government military training was reached with advice from Australia and other countries.

"Now that we have put those plans into action Papua New Guinea is being accused of hiring mercenaries, not trainers, but mercenaries, by the media of a country which endorsed the strategy in the first place," Chan said.
Chan said the Australian comments would put "considerable strain" on the Papua New Guinea-Australia relationship.
Chan said he continued to supported a peaceful solution to the Bougainville crisis.
Hundreds of people have died from the fighting or disease due to a lack of medical supplies in the Bougainville rebellion.
